title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model Serving, Observability, Performance, ADRs
author: Maya Singh
body:
Overview

This page consolidates Redwood Inference's canonical architecture and engineering standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, and performance. It also defines the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process used to capture and approve long-lived technical decisions. Use this as the starting point for teams designing new services or updating existing ones; follow the checklists and link to relevant ADRs before heavy implementation work begins.

Scope
- Applies to all services and components owned by engineering: hosted API, dedicated runtime, private deployment control plane, serving runtime components, and platform tooling.
- Does NOT replace team-level design docs but provides mandatory guardrails and required review points.

1) API Standards
Purpose: Ensure predictable, consistent, and stable public and internal APIs for SDKs, REST endpoints, and async queueing.

Core rules:
- Versioning: All public and internal APIs must use semantic versioning (major.minor.patch). Breaking changes require incrementing the major version and publishing an ADR describing migration plans and rollout strategy.
- API Surface: Prefer explicit resources (e.g., /v1/models/{model_id}/invoke) over RPC-like paths. Keep endpoints narrow and composable.
- Contract-first: For external/public APIs, write an OpenAPI spec before implementation. Internal services should publish a lightweight OpenAPI or JSON schema.
- Pagination & Limits: Use cursor-based pagination for list endpoints. Default max page size = 100, enforce server-side hard limit = 1000.
- Idempotency: Long-running operations and create endpoints must support an idempotency key header (Idempotency-Key).
- Error model: Return structured errors {code, message, request_id, details?}. Map HTTP codes to semantics: 4xx = client input/authorization, 429 = rate limit, 5xx = server. Include request_id in every error for tracing.
- Backwards compatibility: Maintain compatibility for at least 12 months for public APIs or until a deprecation schedule is published.

Example (OpenAPI snippet):
{
  "paths": {
    "/v1/generate": { "post": { "summary": "text generation" } }
  }
}

2) Coding Standards
Purpose: Reliable, readable, and secure code across polyglot stacks.

Language-agnostic guidance:
- Style and linting: Use canonical style guides (PEP8/Black for Python, google-java-format for Java, ESLint + Prettier for JS/TS). CI must fail on lint errors for main branch commits.
- Static analysis: Integrate static analyzers (Bandit, Sonar, ErrorProne, mypy/pyright) configured to at least block high-severity findings.
- Tests: Minimum coverage requirements: new features require unit tests + integration tests. Core services: target 80% coverage on critical modules. All tests run in CI with parallel execution and caching.
- Secrets: Do not hardcode secrets. Use injected secrets (KMS, Vault). Secrets scanning in pre-commit and CI is mandatory.
- Dependency management: Adopt dependency pinning for production images. Monthly automated dependency bump PRs; critical security fixes patched immediately.
- Documentation: Public functions, APIs, and libraries require docstrings and README with examples.

3) Infrastructure Standards
Purpose: Secure, reproducible, and observable infra that supports multi-environment deployments (dev/staging/prod).

Key rules:
- IaC: All infra must be declared in Terraform (preferred) or CloudFormation. No manual console changes without a documented exception and change request.
- Environments: Separate AWS accounts or projects per environment. Enforce network isolation (VPC peering, private subnets) and IAM least privilege.
- Images & Builds: Use immutable infrastructure patterns. Build artifacts in CI (no runtime builds). Base images maintained and scanned weekly.
- Secrets and Keys: Centralized KMS + HSM for production keys. Rotation policy: 90 days for app credentials, 365 days for signing keys unless otherwise required.
- Network: Default deny ingress; allow explicit egress rules. Zero-trust segments for control plane and customer workloads.
- Cost controls: Tagging convention required: team, service, env, cost-center. Set budget alerts per service monthly.

Example Terraform convention record:
| Resource | Tag keys required | Owner |
|---------|------------------|-------|
| aws_ecs_service | team, service, env, cost-center | service-owner@example.com |

4) Model-Serving Standards
Purpose: Ensure models are served reliably, efficiently, and safely across Redwood’s runtime variants.

Serving guidelines:
- Model packaging: Models must include a manifest (manifest.json) with fields: model_id, version, framework, tokenizer_spec, quantization_profile (if any), expected_max_tokens, and compatibility matrix.
- Model validation: Before production rollout, run the model onboarding checklist: unit-level weight checksums, small-batch inference smoke tests, end-to-end accuracy/regression evals (see applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks).
- Runtime compatibility: Declare required runtime features (KV-cache, attention-optimizations, quantized weights). Runtime will map models to supported hardware; if unsupported, the onboarding must add a fallback compatible variant.
- Canary & Rollouts: Deploy new model versions to 1% traffic for 24 hours with automated quality gates (latency, error rate, eval score). If gates pass, increase to 10% for 48 hours, then full rollout. Abort criteria must be defined per rollout.
- Quantization & Profiles: Quantization profiles stored with model manifest. Any quantized variant must have an associated quality regression test.

5) Observability Standards
Purpose: Make systems debuggable and measurable to meet SLOs and accelerate incident resolution.

Metrics & Traces:
- SLOs: All user-facing services must define SLOs and SLIs. Default SLOs for inference API: 99.9% p90 latency per model route <= configured threshold (see Performance), error rate < 0.1% 5xx, availability 99.95% monthly.
- Metrics: Emit standardized metric names: redwood.<service>.<component>.<operation>.<metric>. Use units and labels consistently (latency_ms, tokens_generated, batch_size).
- Tracing: Instrument key code paths with OpenTelemetry. Every external request must propagate trace_id and request_id.
- Logs: Structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, trace_id, model_id, user_org. PII must never be logged (see security-and-compliance/data-management).
- Dashboards & Alerts: Standard dashboard templates per service. Alerting thresholds: page at SLO breach risk (error_budget < 20%) or sustained 5xx rate above 0.5% for 5min.

6) Performance Standards
Purpose: Ensure consistent latency and cost profiles across deployments.

Guidelines & Targets:
- Latency budgeting: Define critical path latency breakdowns (network, runtime scheduling, kernel exec, batching overhead). For hosted low-latency routes target: p50 < 50ms, p90 < 150ms, p99 < 500ms (token-level generation excluding large context workloads). If a route cannot meet targets, document in the service runbook and classify as "latency-optimized" or "throughput-optimized".
- Batching and Caching: Default to smart batching with target end-to-end queuing time <= 20ms under nominal load. KV/prefix caching should be enabled with TTLs defined per model/service.
- Throughput: For Dedicated clusters, document expected tokens/sec per GPU for representative models. Capacity planning should include 25% buffer for burst traffic.
- Benchmarks: Use the canonical benchmarking suite (eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite). Benchmarks must include representative prompt mixes, beam/temperature settings, and end-to-end network overhead.

7) ADR Process (Decision Records)
Purpose: Capture architectural decisions, alternatives considered, the chosen approach, and the consequences. ADRs are the single source of truth for non-trivial, cross-cutting decisions.

Process:
1. Draft ADR using the ADR template in this repo. Title format: ADR-<YYYY-MM-DD>-short-title.
2. Submit as a PR to the architecture-and-standards repo and add reviewers from impacted teams.
3. Public comment window: 5 business days for cross-team review. For high-risk changes allow 10 business days.
4. Approval: Requires at least one architecture steward (eng leads) + owner_team lead approval.
5. Publish: Merge the ADR and update related service docs and confluence links. For breaking ADRs, create a migration plan with milestones.

ADR template (summary):
- Title
- Status (proposed | accepted | superseded | deprecated)
- Context and Problem Statement
- Considered Options
- Decision Outcome and Rationale
- Consequences and Migration Plan
- Owners and Reviewers

Checklist before design/implementation
- [ ] Open API spec or schema for new public endpoints
- [ ] ADR created for breaking or cross-team architectural changes
- [ ] Performance budget and SLOs documented
- [ ] Security review scheduled (if handling PII or sensitive data)
- [ ] Observability plan (metrics/traces/logs + dashboards)
- [ ] Infra IaC changes in a PR with automated plan/apply preview

Governance and Ownership
- Architecture steward: role held by rotating engineering lead(s); contact: architecture-stewards@example.com.
- Service owners: every service must declare an owner in its README and Terraform tags.
- Exceptions: To request an exception to any standard open a change request and include it in the ADR or an exceptions tracker; exceptions must list compensating controls and an expiration date.
